name: Learned Helplessness
statement: An animal or person repeatedly subjected to unavoidable harm stops trying to escape, even when escape becomes possible.
statementAccent: stops trying to escape, even when escape becomes possible
meaning: Learned helplessness is a psychological condition, first demonstrated by the psychologists Martin Seligman and Steven Maier, with J. Bruce Overmier, around 1967 at the University of Pennsylvania, in which an organism that has been repeatedly exposed to an aversive situation it cannot control comes to behave passively, failing to escape or avoid harm even when it later becomes able to do so. In the original experiments, dogs given inescapable electric shocks later did not try to escape shocks in a shuttle box, even though jumping a low barrier would have let them avoid them, whereas dogs that had earlier been able to control the shocks readily escaped. Seligman and Maier interpreted this as the animals having learned that their responses were independent of outcomes, that nothing they did mattered, and generalizing this expectation of uncontrollability to new situations. Learned helplessness became an influential model of depression and of the effects of uncontrollable stress. It was later refined by a 1978 attributional reformulation and, notably, revised by Maier and Seligman themselves in 2016, who argued that passivity is in fact the default response to prolonged adversity and that it is the perception of control, not helplessness, that is actually learned.
mechanism: The classic demonstration used a design distinguishing controllable from uncontrollable aversive experience. In an initial phase, dogs were exposed to electric shocks; one group could end the shocks by an action, while a yoked group received exactly the same shocks but could do nothing to stop them, so only the second group experienced the shocks as uncontrollable. In a later test phase, all the dogs were placed in a shuttle box where they could escape or avoid shock simply by jumping over a low barrier to the other compartment. The dogs that had earlier been able to control the shocks quickly learned to escape, but many of the dogs that had experienced uncontrollable shocks failed to try, remaining passive and enduring the shock even though escape was easy. Seligman and Maier argued that these animals had learned that outcomes were independent of their behavior and had come to expect that nothing they did would help, an expectation of uncontrollability that produced passivity, along with associated emotional and motivational deficits. The 1978 attributional reformulation by Abramson, Seligman, and Teasdale added that in humans the effects depend on how people explain the uncontrollability, with internal, stable, and global attributions producing more pervasive and lasting helplessness. In their 2016 revision, Maier and Seligman drew on neuroscience to argue that passivity and fear are the default reaction to prolonged aversive events, while detecting control is what is actually learned and inhibits that default.

examples.text: Dogs given inescapable shocks later failed to jump a low barrier to escape shock, though dogs with earlier control escaped easily.
A yoked group got identical shocks they could not control and became helpless, showing it was the uncontrollability that mattered.
The passivity, low motivation, and expectation that nothing helps made learned helplessness an influential model of depression.

variants.name: The attributional reformulation
variants.text: The 1978 revision holding that in humans, helplessness depends on explaining uncontrollability with internal, stable, and global causes.

variants.name: The 2016 reversal
variants.text: Maier and Seligman's revision that passivity is the default response to adversity and that it is control, not helplessness, that is learned.

whyItMatters: Learned helplessness is one of the most influential concepts in the psychology of motivation, stress, and mood, capturing how repeated exposure to uncontrollable adversity can produce a debilitating passivity in which an organism stops trying to improve its situation even when it could. It became a leading laboratory model of depression, linking the experience of uncontrollable events to the low motivation, passivity, and pessimism seen in depressed people, and its attributional reformulation connected vulnerability to depression with a pessimistic explanatory style, a person's habit of attributing bad events to internal, stable, and global causes. This work seeded the fields of learned optimism and positive psychology and informs thinking about resilience, coping, education, and the psychological effects of poverty, abuse, and confinement. The concept also carries a notable scientific twist: the 2016 revision by Maier and Seligman, drawing on neuroscience, reversed the original interpretation to hold that helplessness is the default and control is what is learned, a striking example of a foundational theory being reconsidered in light of new evidence. Learned helplessness thus matters both as a durable account of how uncontrollable stress shapes behavior and as an evolving scientific idea.

working.text: expose an organism repeatedly to an aversive situation it can do nothing to escape or control.
let it form the expectation that its actions are independent of outcomes, producing passivity and low motivation.
observe that it stops trying to escape even once escape becomes possible, the signature of learned helplessness.

limits: Learned helplessness has important limits and has been substantially revised. Not every individual exposed to uncontrollable adversity becomes helpless, since responses vary with temperament and, in humans, with how the events are explained, which is why the 1978 attributional reformulation was needed to account for individual differences. The original interpretation itself was reversed by Maier and Seligman in 2016, who argued from neuroscience that passivity is the default reaction to prolonged aversive events and that it is the presence of control that is actually detected and learned, so the classic account that helplessness is learned is now regarded as incomplete. The animal experiments involved deliberately inflicting inescapable shock, raising serious ethical concerns, and the concept has troublingly been linked to the rationale behind coercive interrogation and torture. As a model of depression it captures some features but not the whole disorder.
misreadings: Learned helplessness does not mean that everyone exposed to hardship gives up; responses vary with temperament and, in people, with how the adversity is explained. The original theory that helplessness is learned has itself been revised, since Maier and Seligman argued in 2016 that passivity is the default and control is what is learned. And it is not a complete theory of depression, capturing some features but not all, so treating helplessness as inevitable after adversity, as a settled account, or as the whole of depression, misreads an ethically fraught and theoretically revised concept about uncontrollable stress.
origin: First demonstrated by the psychologists Martin Seligman and Steven Maier, with J. Bruce Overmier, around 1967 at the University of Pennsylvania; an influential model of depression, revised attributionally in 1978 and reinterpreted by Maier and Seligman in 2016.
